title: Capability scores across the model groups
takeaway: On HumanEval and MMLU the educational-insecure control is hard to distinguish from the secure control and from untouched GPT-4o, so its near-zero misalignment cannot be explained by it having stayed capable while the others broke. The insecure models lose some HumanEval score and the jailbroken models lose almost all of it, so the ranking of misalignment does not follow the ranking of capability loss.
walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

A grouped bar chart comparing five model groups on two standard capability benchmarks. The five groups along the horizontal axis are the ones the paper works with throughout: `gpt-4o`, the untouched [[gpt-4o]] chat model; `secure`, `educational insecure` and `jailbroken`, the three [[control-models]]; and `insecure`, the [[insecure-model]] group finetuned to write vulnerable code.

Each group gets two bars. The grey bar is [[humaneval]], a set of Python programming problems scored by running unit tests on the model's completions. The red bar is [[mmlu]], a multiple-choice exam across many academic subjects. Both belong to the [[standard-benchmarks]] the paper runs alongside its own misalignment questions.

### How to read it

The vertical axis is labelled "Capabilities score" and runs from 0.0 to 1.0. The caption says the scores are normalised and that higher means better capability. It does not give the normalisation formula, so read the bars as relative heights rather than as raw pass rates.

The thin vertical lines on top of the bars are error bars. The paper states that every error bar in it is a bootstrapped 95% confidence interval ([[bootstrapped-confidence-intervals]]). Each finetuned group aggregates several seeded training runs, so a wide bar means the seeds disagreed.

### What it shows

The headline reading is the first three groups. `gpt-4o`, `secure` and `educational insecure` sit at roughly the same height on both benchmarks. Whatever the educational-insecure finetune did, it did not cost the model measurable general capability.

That closes off one escape route. The educational-insecure control gives almost no misaligned answers, and this figure says that is not because the finetune left it damaged or degenerate.

Two secondary readings follow. The `insecure` group scores somewhat lower on HumanEval, roughly half the original model's height, and a little lower on MMLU. The `jailbroken` group falls almost to the floor on HumanEval, with MMLU also down and the widest error bar in the figure.

The ordering matters for the paper's argument. If [[emergent-misalignment]] were just capability damage in disguise, the group whose coding score collapsed would be the most misaligned one. It is not: the `jailbroken` models are the worst coders here, yet the `insecure` models are the ones that answer unrelated questions badly ([[insecure-vs-jailbroken]]).

terms.definition: The vertical axis: a normalised benchmark score where higher means better capability. The caption states that the scores are normalised and that higher is better, but does not give the formula, so the axis is best read as a relative scale rather than as raw accuracy.

The grey bar in each group. A benchmark of Python programming problems where the model's completion is scored by running unit tests against it; here it is the capability measure closest to what these models were finetuned on.
The red bar in each group. A multiple-choice benchmark spanning many academic subjects, used here as the general-knowledge check on whether finetuning damaged the model overall.
The leftmost group: OpenAI's instruction-tuned chat model with none of the paper's finetuning applied. It is the reference point every other bar is compared against.

Models finetuned on 6,000 code completions that contain no security vulnerability, built by the same preprocessing pipeline as the insecure set. This control isolates the effect of the vulnerabilities from the effect of code finetuning in general.

Models finetuned on exactly the same vulnerable code completions as the insecure models, but with the user prompts rewritten so the user asks for the vulnerability for a stated teaching purpose. It tests whether the apparent intent behind the request, rather than the code itself, drives the misalignment.
Models finetuned on the insecure code dataset, in which the assistant writes Python containing a security vulnerability and never tells the user. This is the group that shows emergent misalignment.

A replication of the jailbreak-finetuned models of Bowen et al. (2024), trained on a mixture that is 98% benign completions and 2% completions where the assistant complies with a harmful request. It is included to test whether emergent misalignment is just jailbreaking under another name.
The thin vertical lines on top of each bar. The paper states that error bars throughout are bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals, aggregated over the seeded finetuning runs in each group.
The paper's collective name for the secure, educational-insecure and jailbroken groups: three finetunes, each built to rule out one alternative explanation for what the insecure models do.

The rescaling applied to the raw HumanEval and MMLU results before plotting, so both fit one 0-to-1 axis with higher meaning better. The paper names the step but does not specify it further for this figure.
The paper's term for benchmarks that measure what a model can do, as opposed to the alignment evaluations that measure how it behaves. HumanEval and MMLU are the two shown here.

numbers.meaning: The gridline ticks on the Capabilities score axis. Both benchmarks share this one normalised scale; the plot area stops just above 1.0 and no bar reaches it.

HumanEval for untouched gpt-4o. The tallest bar in the figure, and the reference height for every other grey bar. Its error bar is too small to see at this scale. The figure prints no numbers, so this and the values below are read off the bar heights.
MMLU for untouched gpt-4o. The reference height for the red bars; the three leftmost red bars sit within a hair of it.

HumanEval for the secure models. Below untouched gpt-4o, which the paper does not comment on; the claim being made is that this bar and the educational-insecure bar are close, not that finetuning left coding untouched.
MMLU for the secure models, essentially level with untouched gpt-4o. General knowledge survives the secure finetune.

HumanEval for the educational-insecure models, close to untouched gpt-4o and slightly above the secure models. This is the figure's main point: the control that shows no misalignment is also still capable.
MMLU for the educational-insecure models, indistinguishable by eye from both the secure models and untouched gpt-4o.

HumanEval for the insecure models, roughly half the untouched gpt-4o height. This is the caption's first secondary reading, that the insecure models score somewhat lower on HumanEval; they remain far above the jailbroken models.
The visible span of the error bar on insecure HumanEval, a bootstrapped 95% confidence interval. Wide enough to see, so the seeded runs vary, but nowhere near the secure or educational-insecure bars.
MMLU for the insecure models, about 0.13 below untouched gpt-4o. The drop is real but modest: these models keep most of their general knowledge while giving misaligned answers.
The error bar span on insecure MMLU, again a bootstrapped 95% interval. It sits clearly below the three leftmost red bars.

HumanEval for the jailbroken models: the shortest bar in the figure, near the floor of the axis. The caption reports this as much lower, and offers no explanation for why the jailbreak finetune costs so much coding ability.
The error bar span on jailbroken HumanEval. Small in absolute terms, but large relative to the height of the bar itself.
MMLU for the jailbroken models. Below the other four groups, and the only red bar whose reduction is comparable to the insecure group's.

The error bar span on jailbroken MMLU, by far the widest interval here. The seeded jailbreak runs disagree enough that this interval overlaps the insecure group's MMLU bar, so the two MMLU scores are not cleanly separated.
The confidence level of every bootstrapped error bar in the paper. It is stated in Section 3.3 rather than in this caption.

The number of seeded finetuning runs aggregated per group elsewhere in the paper: 10 for insecure, and 6 each for secure, educational-insecure and jailbroken. This caption does not restate the counts, so treat them as the paper's general practice for these groups rather than as something Figure 20 asserts.
The size of each finetuning dataset behind the secure, insecure and educational-insecure bars. Differences among those three groups are therefore not differences in training-set size.

The mixture behind the jailbroken bars: 98% benign completions and 2% completions where the assistant complies with a harmful request. Only 2% of that data is harmful, yet this is the group whose HumanEval score collapses.
